Generally looks good, a few small issues:
* It uses `--library` to omit `main` and generate a `goose_init` itself. Wouldn't it be simpler to just have the `goose_init` call `main`? One less flag, no special requirements, and the programmer gains a way to run custom init code for the DLL.
* This checking against `ckeywords` is a bit unfortunate. I guess this is the only location in the compiler where we emit un-prefixed identifiers, and we want to do so to be compatible with DLL uses that want particular names?
* This is a somewhat niche/specialized feature, thus does not need to be described in the main `README.md`. Maybe move this to a section at the end of the tutorial.

@aardappel Thanks for the review! Addressed all three:

* Dropped `--library`. `--header out.h` now builds for a C host (no C `main`), and `goose_init` runs `fn main()` after initializing the runtime and globals, so `main` doubles as the library's custom init. A second `goose_init` call is a no-op, and a library may omit `main` entirely 
* I initially added `ckeywords` because there are a few names that will cause a C compiler error if used as identifiers but are allowed as idents in Goose code. It's a relatively small static table and an error like `C symbol cannot be a C keyword` at the Goose compiler is (imo) more friendly than malformed code (`const uint8_t * signed(...)`) failing in the user's C compiler. Happy to drop it if you'd still rather not carry it, but I did keep it 
* Removed the README section and moved it to a new tutorial section at the end ("Calling Goose from C"). Spec §7.11 and the flag table in `implementation.md` are updated too
Thanks! 1st user contribution! 🎈

I'm closing this PR. After this change I hit two more TinyCC bugs on macOS arm64, and both are in upstream TinyCC too:

1. Large static variables start with garbage instead of zeros, because the Mach-O writer maps .bss pages from the file.
2. Calls into Apple-compiled code with more than 8 arguments, like glTexSubImage3D, pass the wrong values, because TinyCC doesn't follow Apple's arm64 calling convention.

TinyCC doesn't seem mature enough on macOS. I don't want to keep hunting its bugs, or make Goose more complex to work around them. I'll stay with clang -O0 for debug builds.

# Varint format benchmark — results

Machine: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D, MSVC 19.44 `/O2`, x64, 2026-08-27.
Harness: `varint_bench.cpp` — sequential encode/decode of value arrays, 4x
unrolled, sum-checked, 5:1 read:write weighting. Two working-set sizes:
n=1024 (L1-resident, but small enough that the branch predictor partially
*memorizes* the value sequence across reps — flatters branchy decoders) and
n=65536 (L2-resident, unmemorizable — closest to real one-shot parsing; use
these numbers). Plus one n=4M decode-only run for the bandwidth regime.

Formats: `leb` / `leb_fast1` (ULEB128, branchy), `leb_pext` (branchless LEB
via BMI2 PEXT), `prefix_tz` / `prefix_tz2` (PrefixVarint, length in trailing
zeros; tz2 = table-driven encode), `goose3` / `goose3_msk` (Goose format:
low 3 bits of byte 0 = 8−L, payload = L-byte LE word >> 3; msk = mask-table
decode), `lenbyte` (length byte + payload, full 64-bit), `sqlite`
(SQLite4-style, branchy), `raw_i8..i64` (fixed-size baselines).

## Headline (n=65536, ns/value)

| distribution              | leb dec | goose3 dec | prefix dec | lenbyte dec | goose3 5:1 | leb 5:1 |
|---------------------------|--------:|-----------:|-----------:|------------:|-----------:|--------:|
| all ≤ 4 bits              |   0.24  |    1.21    |    1.49    |     1.08    |    1.13    |  0.25   |
| 99% ≤ 5b, 1% 6–30b        |   0.30  |    1.21    |    1.50    |     1.07    |    1.13    |  0.30   |
| 90% ≤ 7b, 10% 8–20b       |   0.28  |    1.21    |    1.49    |     1.08    |    1.13    |  0.28   |
| uniform 0–20 bits         |   3.52  |    1.21    |    1.49    |     1.09    |    1.13    |  3.49   |
| uniform 0–32 bits         |   4.45  |    1.22    |    1.50    |     1.10    |    1.13    |  4.46   |

Raw fixed-size baselines: 0.08–0.12 ns/val decode at every size and
distribution (SIMD-vectorizable sums) — ~3x faster than branchy LEB on
skewed data, ~10x faster than the branchless formats.

## Break-even sweep (n=65536, decode ns/val)

Distributions "p1% fits 1 leb byte (≤7 bits) / p2% two bytes (8–14 bits) /
p3% three bytes (15–21 bits)", iid random:

| p1/p2/p3   |   leb | leb_fast1 | goose3 | leb B/v | g3 B/v |
|------------|------:|----------:|-------:|--------:|-------:|
| 95/4/1     | 0.361 |     0.341 |  1.195 |    1.05 |   1.21 |
| 90/8/2     | 0.309 |     0.299 |  1.195 |    1.11 |   1.26 |
| 85/11/4    | 0.290 |     0.305 |  1.193 |    1.17 |   1.32 |
| 80/15/5    | 0.408 |     0.339 |  1.207 |    1.22 |   1.38 |
| 75/18/7    | 0.319 |     0.410 |  1.211 |    1.28 |   1.44 |
| 70/21/9    | 1.270 |     1.415 |  1.215 |    1.35 |   1.50 |
| 65/24/11   | 1.767 |     1.904 |  1.200 |    1.41 |   1.56 |
| 60/27/13   | 2.242 |     2.298 |  1.201 |    1.47 |   1.62 |
| 55/30/15   | 2.769 |     2.497 |  1.197 |    1.53 |   1.68 |
| 50/34/16   | 2.742 |     2.960 |  1.208 |    1.59 |   1.74 |
| 45/37/18   | 3.237 |     3.056 |  1.205 |    1.65 |   1.80 |
| 40/40/20   | 3.043 |     2.958 |  1.205 |    1.71 |   1.86 |

There is no gradual crossover: LEB holds ~0.3–0.4 ns (a 3x win) down to 75%
single-byte, then cliffs directly past goose3 at ~70%. The break-even is a
threshold at roughly 70–75% single-byte values (on this Zen 5 predictor;
iid random is the *pessimistic* case — real data with runs/clustering of
similar sizes predicts better at the same fractions).

## Findings

1. **`goose3` is the best branchless format tested.** Flat ~1.21 ns/val
   decode across *every* distribution; beats `prefix_tz` (1.49) and
   `leb_pext` (2.05) outright. Its decode critical path (unaligned load →
   `and 7` → `sub` → advance) is the shortest of the branchless designs.
   The mask-table decode variant is a wash (same speed) — keep the
   two-shift version, which also gives signed for free via arithmetic
   shift.
2. **Branchy LEB is bimodal.** When lengths are predictable (≥90%
   single-byte) the branch predictor makes it ~4x faster than `goose3`
   (0.25–0.30 ns). When lengths are unpredictable it collapses to 3.5–4.5
   ns — 3–4x *slower* than `goose3`. The n=1024 runs show LEB apparently
   winning even on uniform distributions; that is the predictor memorizing
   a 1024-long periodic sequence and does not transfer to real data (the
   n=65536 uniform rows show the truth). SQLite's format behaves like LEB
   (branchy) with no offsetting advantage.
3. **`leb_pext` is a dead end** (~2.05 ns everywhere): PEXT latency sits on
   the serial chain and it caps at 56 bits anyway.
4. **`prefix_tz` decode never beats `goose3`** (tzcnt + longer mask chain),
   and its natural shift-based encode is outright slow (2.3 ns) until
   table-driven (`prefix_tz2`, 0.43 ns). No reason to prefer it: same
   1-byte range as LEB (7 bits) but slower than `goose3` at everything.
5. **`lenbyte` decodes marginally faster than `goose3`** (1.08 vs 1.21 —
   the length byte starts the next-address computation slightly earlier)
   and holds full 64-bit values, but costs a whole extra byte on the tiny
   values that dominate varint use (2.0 vs 1.0 B/val on the tiny
   distribution). Wrong trade for a compression feature.
6. **Bandwidth regime (n=4M, decode-only):** raw_i64 streams at 0.14
   ns/val — hardware prefetch + SIMD keep fixed-size data ~9x faster than
   varint even at 32 MB working set; sequential varint decode is
   latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound, so varint does not overtake i64 on
   pure scans at these sizes. Varint's real win is density: smaller
   structures leave cache for everything else. Encoded sizes: goose3 within
   0.03–0.15 B/val of LEB on skewed data (both ~1.0), ~0.07 larger on
   uniform data, both ~3x smaller than raw_i64 typical.

## Recommendation (adopted)

**ULEB128 wins for Goose's target use case** ("often tiny with outliers"):
it beats the best branchless format ~3x everywhere above ~75% single-byte
values — which covers string lengths, counts, small offsets — and only
loses (up to ~3x) below the ~70% threshold, i.e. on data that arguably
shouldn't be a varint at all. Signed values use zigzag, which costs decode
nothing on the length/advance critical path and restores the full 64-bit
range (goose3's 61-bit cap is gone). `goose3` remains in the benchmark as
the branchless reference should a per-field format choice ever be added
for unpredictable-length data. The raw baselines reconfirm: varint is a
density tool; use fixed storage types when access speed dominates.

> assuming 1 byte is `if ((char)byte > 0) return byte`

That's not how LEB128 works though - the fast path is `if(byte < 128) return byte`. Or maybe I'm misunderstanding what you're saying there.

Either way, now that you mention it, labeling the benchmarks as "tiny", "small", "medium", "large" and "uniform" tells us nothing about the distribution of values (except that the last one is likely uniform u64). And that is suspicious indeed.

Let me look that up...

> | Name | Range | Rationale |
> |------|-------|-----------|
> | tiny (0-247) | Single-byte bijou64 tier | Blob counts, small lengths, enum tags |
> | small (248-64k) | 248 -- 65,535 | Typical payload sizes |
> | medium (64k-4B) | 65,536 -- 4,294,967,295 | Large blob sizes, offsets |
> | large (>4B) | > 2^32 | Content hashes as integers, counters |
> | boundary | All 18 tier-edge values, cycled | Worst-case branch prediction |
> | uniform random | Full u64 range | Unbiased comparison |


https://github.com/inkandswitch/bijou/blob/main/bijoux/benches/SHOOTOUT_ANALYSIS_X86.md

... yeah, I guess your suspicions were warranted.

I thought "tiny" was uniform bytes, which already would be suspicious, but at least that could be chalked up to naivety. But instead it's is specifically the range where bijou64 *always* uses a single-byte. Yeah no shit, of course it encodes/decodes faster if the distribution ensures that the branch predictor is 100% correct for your format, and *only* your format, and it uses half a byte less per value on average.

Similarly, "small" skips 0-248. That effectively removes the "1 byte" branch altogether, but this is true for all compared formats too. However, that also gives bijou64 a stronger branch predictor bias towards 3 bytes (it switches from 2 to 3 bytes for values 504 or up, whereas e.g. LEB128 switches at 16384). Which would explain why performs worse than LEB128 on the encoding side but better on the reading side in their benchmarks: 1/4th of LEB128's values are two bytes instead of three, so that saves significant time on writing. Decoding is just reading, linearly, so less expensive and more dependent on branches.

Besides that, 3 more issues with this PR still:

1. Multiple main functions still pass checking. `fn main() {} fn main(x: i64) {}` succeeds with both `check` and `--check`, but fails with run. The lookup still conflates “missing” with “multiple.” Allow zero candidates while continuing to reject multiple candidates.

Fixed in c0e2297a. The block's `chosen .= p` left `chosen` bound to `json::each`'s parameter class, which each loop pass makes anew, so the binding (and `ps`, storing what it leads to) grew every pass. Calls now map such a binding onto their arguments, as they already did for stores into holders. Any rebind of an outer reference from a block or nested function inside a loop hit this, and the same stale binding also let a reference into a dying local array be returned. Your program now compiles and prints 4.

Fixed in f21573a7. The block parameter `cx` (a struct holding references, passed by value to a function value) started with no contents, so `cx.scratch` was rooted at whichever `u8[>..]` globals the program declared rather than at the caller's `scratch`; that is why the outcome depended on the count. It is now bound to what the argument holds, as a holder variable initialized from it is. The same gap also let a shrink through such a field go unnoticed by the function running the block, which that commit fixes too.

Thanks for the reply.

You're right that writing `each_field` by hand isn't strenuous. I didn't explain it well: the problem isn't the effort of writing it, it's that **it silently goes stale when a field is added**.

Some background. My project is a fairly large \*band-style RPG. Its save format changes often during development, and I plan to keep changing it after release, so saves need to stay readable across versions. `design/serialization.md` deliberately leaves the container format, version included, outside the language, which I think is the right call. But it means keeping old saves readable is the program's job, and what I was after is a feature that makes that job easy to do correctly.

The way I do it is to save each field under a key derived from its name, so that a newer build can read an older save: a field the save lacks keeps its default, and a field the game no longer has is skipped. For that, the save code has to walk every field with its name, and the list must never fall behind the structs.

With a hand-written `each_field`, if I add a field to the struct and forget to add it there too, everything still compiles. That field is then just never saved, and nothing tells you. In my project, the saved state is 5 structs with a few hundred fields, and the fields have been added or changed around 50 times. To avoid exactly this, I currently generate the save code with a Python script that reads the source. With `fields`, the compiler is the only thing that knows the list of fields, so nothing can fall out of sync.

As for languages that have field iteration separate from reflection, two I know of:

- **Nim**'s `fieldPairs`: `for name, value in obj.fieldPairs` walks a field's name and value in declaration order. The loop is unrolled at compile time, one copy per field, and the body is checked at each field's type. It is very close to this proposal. Nim has macros and type introspection on top of that, as separate facilities.
- **D**'s `tupleof`: `foreach (ref f; s.tupleof)` walks the fields, and `__traits(identifier, ...)` gives a field's name.

Zig's `@typeInfo` and C++26's static reflection do the same thing as part of a general reflection feature.

On the relation to a more general reflection feature: I think `fields` could be its smallest piece. It keeps no type information at run time, it is only a compile-time expansion, and what it expands to is ordinary Goose you can write today. A general reflection design would most likely include "walk the fields in order, with their names" anyway, so this form could be matched to it then.

That said, the language design is your call. If you'd rather not add it now, that's fine; I can keep using the generator on my side. Feel free to keep the PR around for reference or to close it.

I left this out of my previous comment, so here is a concrete proposal for the shape of a general reflection feature.

Define reflection as exposing the facts about types that the compiler already knows, only as constants and as rewrites into ordinary code. Types are not values, and no type information is kept at run time. Everything it rewrites to is code you can write in Goose today.

- `fields(v) F`, `fields(&v) F`, `fields(a, b) F`: `F("x", v.x)` for each field; with two values, `F("x", a.x, b.x)`
- `field_count<T>()`: an integer constant
- `type_name<T>()`: a string constant
- `variant_name(v)`: the name of an ADT value's current variant (rewritten into a `match` that returns each variant's name as a string constant)

The structural rendering `print` does today could then be written with these four.

Been thinking about this, and I generally like the direction I think, in particular I like that generating an iteration function like this completely sidesteps the issue of how to access fields from a reflection spec (which would be VERY complicated in Goose).

Thanks for thinking it through. I'm in favor of macros. If what they expand to is ordinary code, type checking and the inference of references keep working as they are. That's the same reason I made `fields` a rewrite.

I think Nim's approach fits Goose best. Nim has two levels: simple hygienic macros (`template`) and macros that build syntax at compile time (`macro`). With a `macro`, compile-time code takes a struct type, reads its fields' names and types, and builds the save and load code as ordinary syntax (`v.turn` and so on). It needs no way to reach a field by name, so it avoids the complexity you mentioned of accessing fields from a reflection spec. The first level, simple substitution, is close to something Goose already has: a function taking a block is already expanded in place.

Why not the other approaches:

- Macros that only match a pattern and substitute, like Scheme's `syntax-rules` or Rust's `macro_rules!`, can't read a struct's fields. The list of fields has to be written out separately, and the problem of forgetting to add a new field there remains.
- Compile-time code that reads type information and reaches a field by name, like Zig's `comptime` with `@field(v, name)`, needs exactly that mechanism for reaching a field by name, which is the complexity you'd like to avoid.

Review of `3fcb3caa3e5b900887ea39169b2aa08c5a280848` (still the PR head when posting). I would address the ABI issue before merging. There are five findings below, followed by a separate `ffi` safety design concern.

Validation: the PR builds with MSVC, its `test/extern_dylib.py` integration test passes on Windows, and its syntax fixture passes roundtrip/check. Additional probes reproduced the Windows loader, sidecar, escaping, and `ffi` cases below. The System V ABI finding was verified using the generated Goose C and Clang 22's Linux-target LLVM output, without executing a Linux binary. The older-glibc link failure is an inspection finding. The full suite was not run.

**1. [P1] Matching struct byte layout with `pad` does not guarantee matching the C calling convention.**

[The dynamic function-pointer declaration](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/3fcb3caa3e5b900887ea39169b2aa08c5a280848/src/codegen_calls.h#L129-L140) uses the ordinary Goose C type. [The new documentation](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/3fcb3caa3e5b900887ea39169b2aa08c5a280848/docs/reference.md#L3722-L3727) recommends matching a native struct with `pad`, but those pads become actual integer array members, which can change ABI classification even when size and offsets match.

For example, a native library has `struct { float x; double y; }`. This Goose declaration compiles:

```goose
struct Mixed { x: f32, pad 4, y: f64 }
extern "foreign" { fn take(p: Mixed) -> f64; }
fn main() { print(take(Mixed { 1.0, 2.0 })); }
```

`goose -o aggregate.c aggregate.goose` emits the equivalent of this packed type:

```c
struct Mixed_g {
    float x_g;
    uint8_t gs_pad0[4];
    double y_g;
};
static double (*gs_dl0_take)(Mixed_g);
```

A small independent ABI probe, `abi.c`:

```c
typedef struct { float x; double y; } Natural;
#pragma pack(push, 1)
typedef struct { float x; unsigned char pad[4]; double y; } Padded;
#pragma pack(pop)
double natural(Natural p) { return p.x + p.y; }
double padded(Padded p) { return p.x + p.y; }
```

```sh
clang --target=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -S -emit-llvm -O2 abi.c -o abi.ll
```

Observed lowered signatures:

```llvm
define dso_local double @natural(float %0, double %1)
define dso_local double @padded(i64 %0, double %1)
```

The native library expects floating-point register arguments; the Goose declaration supplies an integer component and a floating-point component. Calling through that pointer can silently pass incorrect values. Direct binding needs ABI-compatible aggregate types, or the affected shapes must require an adapter and the documentation must say so. The integration test's all-integer `Point` does not exercise this distinction.

**2. [P2] A bundled Windows DLL cannot find a sibling DLL it depends on.**

[The loader calls `LoadLibraryW`](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/3fcb3caa3e5b900887ea39169b2aa08c5a280848/src/runtime/runtime_os.h#L570-L578). Resolving the top-level DLL to an absolute resource path does not add its directory to dependency lookup. This breaks the normal deployment of a library and its dependencies together under `lib/` or `bin/`.

Minimal fixture:

```c
/* lib/dep.c */
__declspec(dllexport) int pr59_dep(void) { return 42; }
```

```c
/* lib/top.c */
__declspec(dllimport) int pr59_dep(void);
__declspec(dllexport) int answer(void) { return pr59_dep(); }
```

```goose
// loader.goose, in the directory above lib/
extern "lib/pr59top" { fn answer() -> i32; }
fn main() { print(answer()); }
```

From the fixture directory in an x64 MSVC developer shell, with `lib/` absent from `PATH`:

```bat
cl /nologo /LD lib\dep.c /Fe:lib\pr59dep.dll /Fo:lib\dep.obj /link /IMPLIB:lib\pr59dep.lib
cl /nologo /LD lib\top.c lib\pr59dep.lib /Fe:lib\pr59top.dll /Fo:lib\top.obj
goose --jit loader.goose
```

Observed: `cannot load lib/pr59top (.../lib/pr59top.dll): Windows error 126`. Both DLLs exist. The native executable fails the same way; the tested native path emitted C and linked the separate runtime object. An equivalent native reproduction is:

```bat
goose -o loader.c loader.goose
goose --emit-runtime runtime.c
cl /nologo /O2 loader.c runtime.c /Fe:loader.exe
loader.exe
```

As a control, loading that same absolute DLL path with `LoadLibraryExW` using `LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR | LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS` succeeds and `answer()` returns 42. Use a dependency-aware load for resolved paths. [Microsoft documents the dependency search behavior here.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/dlls/dynamic-link-library-search-order)

**3. [P2] Sidecar validation rejects valid mappings belonging to unimported package modules.**

[The validation searches `ast.functions`](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/3fcb3caa3e5b900887ea39169b2aa08c5a280848/src/main.cpp#L451-L465), which contains only parsed modules. A package-level mapping can therefore be valid for a module of the package but rejected when a consumer does not import that module.

Fixture layout:

```text
app/main.goose
pkgs/optional/optional.goose
pkgs/optional/optional.build
pkgs/optional/extra.goose
```

```goose
// pkgs/optional/optional.goose
namespace optional;
fn pure() -> i32 { 42 }
```

```goose
// pkgs/optional/extra.goose
namespace optional;
extern "extra" { fn foreign() -> i32; }
```

```text
// pkgs/optional/optional.build
dylibs = ["extra=./extra"];
```

```goose
// app/main.goose
import optional from "../pkgs/optional";
fn main() { print(optional::pure()); }
```

`goose --check app/main.goose` fails with:

```text
optional.build: dylibs maps extra, which no extern block of the package names
```

Adding `import optional.extra;` to the application makes the same check pass, even though the application calls no foreign function. Package configuration should not force every consumer to import every optional binding module. Validate against the package's declaration inventory, or tolerate mappings unused by this compilation.

**4. [P2] Dumping an extern block does not escape its library name.**

[This append writes the decoded library string directly between quotes](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/3fcb3caa3e5b900887ea39169b2aa08c5a280848/src/dump.h#L730-L733).

`escaped.goose`:

```goose
extern "bin\\example" { fn answer() -> i32; }
fn main() {}
```

```sh
goose --check escaped.goose
goose --roundtrip --check escaped.goose
```

The first command passes. The second dumps `extern "bin\example" {`, reports `unknown escape sequence: \e`, and in the Windows Debug build exits with `0xC0000005` after the parse errors. No actual DLL is needed because the function is unused. Use the existing `EscapeString` helper when writing the library name.

**5. [P2] The Python toolchain is missing the new Linux `-ldl` dependency.**

The PR adds `-ldl` in the compiler's `Builder::SystemLibs`, but [the Python `CC.compile` path](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/3fcb3caa3e5b900887ea39169b2aa08c5a280848/scripts/toolchain.py#L303-L307) still appends only `-pthread -lm`. That path is used by the test and benchmark runners. The new runtime object contains `dlopen`/`dlsym`/`dlerror` references even for programs that do not use dynamic externs.

On a glibc system older than 2.34, the expected failure can be isolated with a trivial `app.goose` containing `fn main() { print(42); }`:

```sh
goose -o app.c app.goose
goose --emit-runtime runtime.c
cc app.c runtime.c -pthread -lm -o app
# Missing libdl references; adding -ldl supplies them.
```

This is an inspection finding, not a test executed on an older-glibc machine. Newer glibc systems conceal the missing link dependency because these functions are in libc. Please add the Linux library to the Python compilation path too.

**Separate design concern: the `ffi` module exposes unchecked arbitrary-address reads through the standard library.**

[These signatures accept a plain `u64` address and, for `bytes`, a caller-supplied length](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/3fcb3caa3e5b900887ea39169b2aa08c5a280848/stdlib/ffi.goose#L9-L13). There is no provenance or bounds information attached to either.

`ffi_wild.goose`:

```goose
import ffi;
fn main() { print(ffi::bytes(1, 1).len); }
```

```sh
goose --check ffi_wild.goose
goose --jit ffi_wild.goose
```

The check passes; the run exits with `0xC0000005` on Windows. This requires no user-written extern declaration, native library, or C code. A non-null invalid address is not reported through the API's boolean result, and a valid address with an excessive length can read beyond the foreign allocation.

This behavior is documented and intentional, so I am raising it as an explicit safety/API decision rather than an undocumented implementation accident. Copying foreign memory into Goose-owned storage does not make the source read safe. I would decide how an unchecked pointer API fits Goose's memory-safety promise before including it in the standard library: for example, keep it behind an explicit unsafe/trusted-FFI boundary, or provide library-specific adapters with enforceable pointer and length contracts. Opaque handles alone do not establish readable extent or lifetime.

Review by Claude Code at aardappel's request, measuring how general the speedup is: master (94cc64da) against this branch, generated C compiled with the same flags on both sides, user-space instruction and cycle counts from `perf_event_open`, min of 5 interleaved runs. Machine: Ryzen 9 9950X3D, WSL2 Ubuntu, clang 20.1.8.

### Where it fires

The generated C differs in 8 of the 710 files under test/, samples/, bench/ and stdlib/ at -O1 (the same 8 at -O2): the new test, two existing codegen fixtures, and these programs:

| program (-O2) | functions changed | fields hoisted | reload statements |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| bench/kostya (LangArena, 37 benchmarks in one C file) | 25 | 52 | 34 |
| goose-compress `bench/bench.goose` at `0584d3d^` | 8 | 12 | 36 |
| test/goose_in_goose | 7 | 8 | 50 |
| bench/kostya2 primes | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| samples/31_mini_doom | 2 | 2 | 3 |
| samples/14_bst | 1 | 1 | 0 |

So the pattern is general enough in principle: a loop that reads a field through a reference while storing bytes (a `u8[>..]` builder, a `bool[>..]` sieve) or calling anything, which is exactly what C's TBAA and LICM cannot see through. But most of the LangArena sites are setup loops around `next_int`, not the timed loops.

### What it buys

goose-compress at `0584d3d^`, gzip of a 1.45 MB JSON file, clang -O2. Three code-placement variants (`-falign-functions=64`, `=4096`, `-O3`) gave the same picture:

| | instructions | cycles |
|---|---:|---:|
| level 1, 30 runs | 1,576M → 1,556M (−1.3%) | 518M → 519M (+0.1% to +0.4%) |
| level 6, 5 runs | 601M → 588M (−2.1%) | 198M → 193M (−1.3% to −2.4%) |

LangArena, all 50 benchmarks of run.js with the Makefile's flags: total instructions unchanged to under 0.1%, and 41 of the 50 have byte-identical counts. The moves: Nbody −3.4% instructions (−0.7% cycles), Graph BFS/DFS/AStar −0.4% to −0.5%, Template::Parse −0.7%, TextRaytracer +1.1%, Calculator::Ast +0.9%, Maze::AStar +0.9%. Cycle deltas elsewhere are within this machine's ±3% placement noise.

kostya2 primes: identical instruction count (416M), so clang was already keeping `s.limit` out of the hot loops there.

The M1 numbers in the description (−8% instructions, −3% cycles) are larger than what x86 shows; part of that is x86 folding a load into the instruction that uses it, so a removed load is often not a removed instruction. Either way, on x86 this is a 0–2% win on the program it was written for and a wash on the rest of the corpus.

### Soundness

I found nothing wrong. The suite passes here (Windows, compiler without builtin packages). A probe with store shapes the test does not cover (a multi-assign to the field, a `for &x` binder over the array the reference points into, a whole-element store into that array, a nested function storing through a free variable, a store through a slice of the array, a scalar reference to the field bound before the loop, and a loop inside an inlined callee bound to an element) prints the same on master and this branch at -O0/-O1/-O2. Byte stores not invalidating the cache is the main gain over TBAA and is what the spec's typed-memory rule guarantees; nullable references are excluded by `IsPlainRef`; function-value bodies are reached through `RunChildren`; format overloads, dispatch, externs and the thread builtins all reload.

### Where it costs

Two choices make it reload more than it needs to, and in one benchmark that is a net loss:

1. An extern summarizes as "may store anything", and `sqrt`, `sin` and friends are externs. In TextRaytracer `s.w` was read once per row; now it is reloaded after every `gs_sqrt` and every `intersect_sphere` call per pixel (the +1.1%). Nbody's inner loop reloads all four cached fields after each sqrt (clang removes most of those). An extern whose parameters are all scalars cannot store to Goose memory in any way the rest of codegen admits — `EmitExternCall` already syncs stacks only when the extern grows one — so `SpecStores` could give those an empty summary.
2. The in-progress placeholder in `SpecStores` makes every function in a recursive cycle, a self-recursive one included, summarize as "may store anything". Since `recursive` is the main way a function stays out of line, that hits exactly the calls left in loops: in goose_in_goose's recursive-descent parser every call reloads `ctx.cursor` (50 reload statements for 8 hoisted fields). Under clang the dead reloads vanish; under TinyCC (`goose run`) each is a real load and store. A two-phase summary (local stores per spec, then a transitive closure over callees) fixes this and drops the placeholder trick in about the same number of lines.

With (1) fixed the eager reload after calls should mostly stop adding loads; if it still can, a cheap guard is not to cache a field that the body reads fewer times than it has may-store call sites.

### Complexity

About 340 lines of compiler code, self-contained, shaped like the three hoisting mechanisms §6.10 already has (views, field views, divisors), so it is less than the diff size suggests. What I would change before landing:

- `CacheFieldReads`' walk duplicates `HoistDivisors`' walk almost line for line (inner binders from VarDecl/ForLoop/MatchExpr/fvparams, Assign/IncDec/`BF_WRITE` stores, FnDecl/FunVal skipped). One walk over the loop body yielding binders and stores, used by both, removes some 40 lines and keeps the two from drifting apart.
- `FieldReadRoot`/`FieldKey`/`FieldReadKey` are `FieldRoot`, the `fieldviews` key and `UseFieldView`'s path walk with `fieldbound` added; folding `fieldbound` into `FieldRoot` would let the field views see the same roots.
- `SpecStores` is the genuinely new and reusable piece (`HoistDivisors`' "no reference anywhere in the function" rule could use it later).

### Bottom line

Sound, and it matches a real pattern, but as measured it is worth 0–2% on goose-compress and nothing across the rest of the corpus, for a fourth hoisting mechanism in codegen. I would want (1) and (2) and the shared walk before landing. The write-back variant (keeping fields the loop stores to in locals, what the second commit documents doing by hand) is where bigger wins would be, but the description's own table shows it adding only 0.2% on the matcher, so it does not obviously justify more complexity either.
Agreed, the gains are smaller than I expected for how much code this adds. Closing it.

1. **Cancellation and overflow.** stdlib.md now says the two roundings can differ by far more than the last bit, with both of your cases: cancellation (the `2^-60` against `0.0` example, which can flip a branch) and intermediate overflow (`mul_add(1e308, 2.0, -1e308)` is `1e308` fused, `inf` unfused). Spec §7.12 says the same in one sentence. `stdlib_math` now checks the overflow case at both widths accepts exactly those two results.

2. **Helpers.** stdlib.md now says that only calls Goose emits in the `simd fn`'s own body fuse, so moving a `mul_add` into a plain helper can change the result and the speed between `-O0` and `-O2`. Checking this showed an `inline fn` helper doesn't fuse at `-O0` either, since nothing is inlined there (spec §7.13), and the docs say so. `simd_mul_add` now reports five calls: a plain function, and in a `simd fn` a direct call, an `inline fn` helper, a plain helper and a function value. `clang_mul_add` generates the C at Goose `-O2` and `-O0`. At `-O0` the runner requires both helpers to round as a plain function and the direct call and function value to fuse; at `-O2` the inline helper must fuse too, and the plain helper may go either way.

3. **Function values.** You're right: they're resolved at compile time, so the call names the macro and fuses like a direct call, at `-O0` too. I corrected the implementation notes and the `runtime_ext.h` comment: the function definition is only for C that names it without the macro, which the generated code never does. I'm not a Goose maintainer, so take this as one random user's thoughts:

I think Goose needs TLS in its stdlib, and eventually HTTP too. goose-tls can't be that (it needs OpenSSL installed).

I like that it follows Go's crypto/tls so closely. It's a good model, and it makes the code easy to check against Go's.

A few things I think would help:

- Conformance tests. Go runs BoringSSL's BoGo suite against crypto/tls, and [tlsfuzzer](https://github.com/tlsfuzz/tlsfuzzer) finds alert and state-machine bugs that interop tests can't, since a well-behaved peer never sends bad input. [Wycheproof](https://github.com/C2SP/wycheproof)'s vectors catch edge cases in the primitives that standard test vectors miss.
- Fuzzing the parsers (records, the hello messages, asn1, x509) on a native build with libFuzzer and sanitizers.
- Checking constant time in the compiled code. Goose goes through a C compiler, which can turn masks back into branches at `-O2`. Running the native build under Valgrind with secrets marked as undefined (as ctgrind does), or under [dudect](https://github.com/oreparaz/dudect), would back up what the README says.
- Windows. Go supports it, so it should be doable. `getentropy` doesn't exist there (Go uses `ProcessPrng`, and `BCryptGenRandom` is the documented API), and x509 can't load Windows' system roots yet.

On performance:

- Benchmarks in the repo would help: handshakes per second, throughput per suite, and memory per connection, against OpenSSL with and without AES-NI.
- Some gains are possible in plain Goose. `seal_record` and `open_record` allocate a new buffer for every record, and the key schedule runs one-shot HMACs. Decrypting in place and keeping HMAC state between derivations both help, and ChaCha20 over several blocks at once may vectorize under `simd fn`.
- AES-GCM is harder. Without AES-NI and carry-less multiply it will stay well behind OpenSSL, and Goose can't reach those instructions today.
  - Go uses assembly for those paths and keeps the portable code as the fallback. A small C kernel using intrinsics could do the same here, with the bitsliced code kept for other CPUs, if a little C is acceptable in the stdlib (it already has some, for `popcount` and the byte search).
  - Intrinsics in Goose itself would be the cleaner fix, so this is only worth it if they aren't coming soon. @aardappel, are they on the near-term roadmap?

Reviewed e09fe18e. The core NEON support looks worthwhile and reasonably compact; I found no correctness blockers. Most of the apparent size is generated code and tests: of 429 added lines, 137 are generated runtime text and 137 are tests. The runtime source itself has 130 additions and 22 deletions.

Three suggestions:

1. **Consider separating the 64-byte scan optimization from the basic NEON support.** [`GS_ANY_WIDE`](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/e09fe18e6aa586bccc26a70a1d7913e11daf594e/src/runtime/runtime_impl.h#L1458-L1472) tests four blocks before checking whether the first contains a match, so it adds work for frequent matches. The reported sparse-search improvement is promising, but the benchmarks for other set types compare against the scalar implementation rather than isolating 16-byte versus 64-byte NEON. In an isolated ARM64 Clang 22 `-O2` compilation of the scan code, retaining the wide loop increased the text size from 4,610 to 5,618 bytes. It would help to compare the two NEON versions for frequent, rare, and absent matches across the set kinds before retaining the wide loop for all of them. This is an optimization tradeoff, not a demonstrated performance regression.

2. **Remove the redundant mask in the NEON bit-table lookup.** [Line 1440](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/e09fe18e6aa586bccc26a70a1d7913e11daf594e/src/runtime/runtime_impl.h#L1440) can use `vqtbl1q_u8(m->c, vshrq_n_u8(x, 4))`. The index is already 0-15, and the table repeats after eight entries. I checked equivalence for all 256 byte values; Clang currently emits the unnecessary AND.

3. **If keeping the wide loop, add a few tests that reach a second 64-byte iteration.** The [new lengths](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/e09fe18e6aa586bccc26a70a1d7913e11daf594e/test/stdlib/stdlib_byteset_blocks.goose#L86-L88) stop at 79, and the existing byte-set tests stop at 100. A few targeted cases at 128 bytes and beyond, with later matches, competing matches across blocks, and no match, would cover this without expanding the exhaustive test matrix much.

The rest seems justified: the NEON comparisons/table lookup, nibble mask replacing movemask, and small abstractions that keep the search loops shared with x86. I'd keep the exhaustive tests.

The Unicode issue is real, but I would revise the argument-capture approach before merging.

**Quoting regression in `src/runtime/runtime_os.h:16`:** `CommandLineToArgvW` does not implement the modern CRT's argument-parsing rules. I reproduced this on Windows using the raw command-line suffix `"a""b" c`:

- CRT: two arguments, `a"b` and `c`.
- `CommandLineToArgvW`: one argument, `a"b c`.

This changes argument contents and count even for ASCII input. The new test passes argument lists through Python's standard escaping, which does not exercise this spelling. Please preserve CRT quoting semantics and add a raw-command-line regression case.

Windows normally supplies a UTF-16 command line, while ordinary narrow `argv` uses the process ANSI code page and can lose characters before `main`. Other language runtimes handle this too: [Python uses `wmain`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Programs/python.c), while [Go](https://go.dev/src/os/exec_windows.go) and [Rust](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/main/library/std/src/sys/args/windows.rs) read the wide command line and parse it themselves. Rust explicitly avoids Shell32 because of loading overhead and its different quoting rules.

Shell32 here is a Windows DLL dependency, not a command-shell invocation, but it is not required for Unicode arguments. Two alternatives seem worth considering:

- For `goose build`, extend the compiler's existing UTF-8 manifest approach to generated executables. On Windows 10 1903+, this selects the process code page before CRT startup, allowing ordinary `argv` with compatible runtimes. This would need validation across the supported C backends, and does not by itself cover standalone C compiled without the manifest. [Microsoft documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/globalizing/use-utf8-code-page).
- For standalone generated C, use a Windows `wmain` wrapper and convert its wide arguments for Goose. That preserves CRT parsing and avoids Shell32, although entry-point setup varies by toolchain.

Initializing arguments before globals and preserving explicitly supplied JIT/embedding vectors are both appropriate. I would retain those properties while avoiding a second parser with different semantics.

One more use case for this: reading a text file **line by line** when the file is too large, or too long-running, to hold in memory. Examples are logs, CSV or TSV exports, word lists, and other line-oriented data.

Today `os` can read lines only from stdin (`read_line`). For a named file, a program has two choices: `read_file` the whole thing, so its memory is the size of the file, or bring its own C through `extern fn` as in option 3.

Goose's slices make line reading very cheap once there is a way to read in pieces. You need one fixed buffer and three steps:

1. Fill the buffer with the next chunk of the file.
2. Hand on each complete line as a slice into the buffer. Nothing is copied.
3. Move the cut-off last line to the front of the buffer, then refill.

After the buffer is allocated, nothing more is allocated however long the file is, and memory stays at the buffer size. All of this can be written in Goose on top of the read primitive in option 1 or 2. Only the chunked read needs the runtime.

It would help if the standard library also had the line loop itself, for example:

```goose
// F(line) for each line of the file, without its "\n" (or "\r\n");
// false if the file cannot be read.
fn each_line<F>(path: const u8[:], max_line: i64 = 65536) -> bool
```

The line passed to the block would be a slice into the reader's buffer, valid only for that call, as `csv::each_record` already does with its fields. `max_line` bounds the buffer, and a longer line would be a reported error. A block form also means the file is closed when the loop ends, so the caller never handles a `File`.

On mmap: it would suit random access to regular files well, and `each_split(mapped, '\n')` over a mapping would give the same loop. A sequential chunked read would still be needed for:
- files that cannot be mapped, such as pipes, FIFOs, `/dev/stdin` and some special files;
- programs that want a fixed memory budget instead of letting the page cache decide.

So option 1 or 2 plus an `each_line` built on it would still be worth having next to mmap.

Definitely want some form of this idea to be added: it further expands Goose's "flat data structure" abilities.

In terms of `mmap`: on the one hand would seem to fit nicely with Goose, which already does a bunch of address space mapping.

On the other hand it doesn't, because currently all memory accessible by say, a slice, must point to memory owned by Goose arrays and must have compiler checked lifetimes. This means we can't refer to memory allocated outside of Goose, much like how Goose currently can't refer to memory allocated by external C libraries.

Clearly, we don't want any copying involved in accessing the `mmap` memory.

I can imagine hacky solutions, where `mmap` functionality would effectively would allocate a special purpose Goose stack with arbitrary size different from the default stack size, and tied to a Goose array. But that feels very special purpose.

Wasm support is not a simple fix, see here for context: https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/master/docs/design/wasm.md

This language derives a lot of its power from being able to reserve large amounts of address space, which pretty much requires a 64-bit system, and one with address space reservation functionality (which even wasm64 can't currently do).

Making the above suggested fixes doesn't help with that, you'd just end up with a Goose program with tiny stacks that would run out (if it would work at all).

Thanks, both good questions. I've reworked the draft PR (#161) around the first one.

**`assert` as the base.** You're right that `assert` already carries the meaning, so a clause now means exactly what an `assert` at the same place means:

- `requires p` is `assert(p)` on entry, `ensures q` is `assert(q)` at each return, and `invariant i` is `assert(i)` at the head of each iteration.
- Every build checks it, like an assert, and the code after it can rely on it: it narrows, and BCE uses it as a fact. So a `requires` does what an entry `assert` does in a `checkfree` function today; the PR has a test where a `requires` is what makes a `checkfree` function verify.
- A check whose condition the existing BCE facts already settle is removed, the same way a proved bounds check is. This applies to plain `assert`s too, so proofs only ever remove checks and never change what a program does. (I first had contracts as debug-only checks. That meant they couldn't safely give BCE facts, which was the wrong trade.)

So why keep `requires`/`ensures` at all? They don't add meaning; they say *where* a fact belongs, which is the function's interface. Today a function's entry facts come from its call sites, so a new caller elsewhere can break a `checkfree` function. With `requires`, each caller is checked against the clause and the body is checked once. A proved `ensures` can become a fact at every call site without reading the body. `result` and `old(e)` exist only because a postcondition has to name them. The PR doesn't do the caller side yet; for now both are facts inside the function.

`invariant` and `implies` are much weaker cases. `invariant` could just be an `assert` at the head of the loop body, given a defined meaning (it also holds when the loop exits), and `implies` is just `!a || b`. I'm happy to drop both if you'd rather keep the keyword count down.

The trade-off of checking everywhere is cost: an unproved quantifier is a loop in every build, so `requires sorted(a)` makes a binary search linear. The options I see:

- a per-clause marker that checks only in debug builds and gives no facts;
- a build flag that does the same for all clauses;
- leaving the cost visible until a proof removes it.

I'd value your take on which.

**External provers.** Fair point: I stated it as a feature without arguing for it. I agree the compiler itself should be the product: the existing difference-constraint analysis first, then (later) an SMT solver. External provers are only a fallback for proofs no built-in solver will get, such as non-linear arithmetic, floating-point error bounds, induction over recursive data, or real algorithm correctness. Lean lets a person, or increasingly an LLM, write those proofs, and its maths library already holds much of what they need. Building anything like that into the compiler would go against its small, dependency-free design; even an SMT solver would probably run as a separate process. So: rarely needed, the last phase, and fine to cut. The rest of the proposal doesn't depend on it.

This is my exploration of the subject, doesn't go as far in proof direction, but all very pragmatic stuff: https://aardappel.github.io/goose/docs/design/llm_frontier.html

And yes I now see that `assert` alone doesn't cover it.

Thanks for the detailed report, but it does not match the compiler as released.

**The flags quoted are not Goose's.** `Builder::CFlags()` in `src/build.h` has never returned `-O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer`; in every release and on master it gives gcc-style toolchains `-O2` only (`goose build -v` prints the exact command lines). Without an AVX flag GCC generates no ymm code, so a `vmovdqa %ymm0, ...` cannot appear in a `goose build` executable.

**The repro does not compile.** `pad` is a Goose keyword, so `fn call_chain(pad: u64, ...)` is a parse error. With the parameter renamed, the C that Goose generates for it contains no ymm instruction at all even when compiled with `gcc -O3 -march=native` (also with `-mabi=ms`), so the disassembly shown is not from this program.

**The GCC bug itself is real, but Goose is not exposed to it.** It is [GCC PR 54412](https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=54412), open since 2012 and fixed in September 2026 for GCC 17 (MSYS2's GCC has carried a downstream patch for years). It affects over-aligned stack objects: `__m256` values passed by value, the hidden copies the MS ABI makes for by-reference arguments, and over-aligned temporaries. Goose's generated C never passes or returns 32-byte vector types and declares its vector types `aligned(1)`, so even a package compiled with `-mavx2` does not hit it. `-mstackrealign` would not help either: on SEH targets GCC never realigns the stack pointer, which is why the upstream fix aligns each object's address instead. Anyone adding AVX flags of their own to an unpatched GCC 16 or older can pass `-Wa,-muse-unaligned-vector-move`.

**The stack reserve is a fair point.** A built executable currently gets the platform default (1 MB on Windows) while `goose run` gives a program 64 MB. That is being looked at separately from this issue.

If you do see a crash from an unmodified `goose build`, please attach `goose version`, the command lines from `goose build -v`, and the disassembly of the faulting function including its name and prologue, and I will reopen.

Thanks for the detailed report, it made the problem easy to pin down.

**What was wrong on our side.** A `--header` build had a `goose_init` but no way to end the program. Each reload therefore called the new image's `goose_init` over the old one's, and the old image's data stack regions were never released: at the default 2 GB reservation per region, that is the ~4 GB of virtual address space per reload you measured. With the runtime object shared between images it was worse than a leak: the second `gs_rt_start` installed the fault handler over itself, so a real crash in a reloaded program would have looped instead of crashing.

**Fixed in 261a2daa.** Library builds now have `goose_exit()`, declared in the header next to `goose_init`. It releases everything the start set up: main's stack block, the data stack regions, the queues, and the fault handling (the SIGSEGV/SIGBUS handlers that were installed before are restored, or the vectored handler removed on Windows). After it, `goose_init` can start a program again, this image or another one. So a reload is:

1. compile the edited `.goose` to C to a `.so`, `dlopen` it and resolve the entry points (a failure here leaves the old image untouched);
2. `goose_exit()` on the old image, then `dlclose` it;
3. `goose_init()` on the new image.

The region count no longer grows, so the `gs_rt_init(..., 64, ...)` edit is not needed. If a host calls a second image's `goose_init` without having called `goose_exit` on the first, the runtime now stops with `a program is already started in this process: call its goose_exit first` rather than silently dropping the registry. `goose_exit` is a runtime error while a worker of the program is still running, since nothing can release a running worker's storage.

**Demo B / Experiment C.** I'm not going to support transplanting globals between images, nor the `memoryhandle` / `can_safely_hotreload` / `goose_reinit` API. The report lists the reasons itself: the generated field names and layout are private, a size check is not a layout check, and no amount of generated layout metadata or migration hooks makes copying raw stack pointers between two images' initializations safe. That is not a hot-reload contract I want to maintain.

The supported way to get B's behaviour (particles survive, color edits apply) is the usual one for hot reloading: keep the state that has to survive in memory the host owns, and hand it to the image on every call. Exported functions take `T&` and `T[:]` parameters, so the host can own the particle buffer (a slice of a fixed-capacity array plus a count, and the cursor, pressed state and tick count beside it) and pass them to `goose_update` / `goose_draw`, while the image holds only code and its `let` constants. Then `goose_exit` + `goose_init` is the reload: the new colors apply because `goose_init` runs the global initializers again, the particles live on because the image never owned them, and nothing depends on the layout of `gs_globals_t`.

While testing this I also found that an export taking or returning an `i64` was declared with a type the header never defined; the header now carries the runtime's scalar aliases.

   A default sees the parameter names, so in `file: u8[:] = file()` the name `file` is the parameter, not the builtin. The same signature is the example in `docs/reference.md` and in the design note. `scripts/check_doc_examples.py docs/reference.md` also fails on the new reference block, because it has no body: it needs `{}` or a `<!-- fragment -->` marker. With the parameters renamed (`f`, `row`), everything works as described, including a defaulted call into a namespaced function in another module and calls inside a loop.

2. **The names.** The PR's own example collides, which shows that `file` and `line` are risky names for global builtins. Both are among the most common local and parameter names (`for line in lines`), and every scope that declares one loses the builtin. Builtin names are hard to change once code uses them, so it would be good to settle this before merge. A less collision-prone name would avoid the problem, for example `src_file()`/`src_line()`, or a single builtin that returns both.

3. **Which file string.** `file()` returns the base name, but runtime aborts already print the source path (`CodeGen::FileRef`, which emits one static string per file). Log lines and aborts from the same program would name the file differently, and two `util.goose` files in different directories look the same. Reusing `FileRef`'s string would keep the two consistent and avoid emitting a new literal at every call. If the base name is the intended choice, for example to keep paths out of binaries, that's fine, but it is semantics people will come to rely on, so it's worth deciding on purpose.

Minor: `StampLocBuiltins` matches by spelling, so it also restamps a zero-argument user function named `file` or `line`. That only moves where its diagnostics point, so it's harmless. Initial review by claude-opus-5-5:

The bound counts tree depth rather than the recursion that overflows. As a result it rejects ordinary programs that master compiles, mostly the kind of code generators write, and it still misses one of the crashes it targets. I measured Windows Release builds of this branch (76f67ba7) and of master (eee6f2d0):

| input | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `x + 1 + 1 + …`, 1,500 terms | compiles and runs (also at 5,000; `check` is fine at 20,000) | `expression nested more than 1000 levels deep` |
| `if … else if …`, 1,500 arms | compiles and runs (also at 5,000; `check` is fine at 10,000) | same error |
| 1,000 `guard` statements in one function | compiles and runs | same error |
| `!` repeated 200,000 times | crashes | still crashes, in the parser |

1. Left-associative binary chains and `else if` chains don't recurse in the parser: `ParseBinary` loops, and `ParseIf` calls itself, not `ParsePrimary`. They are still deep trees, though, so `cur.nodepath` passes 1000 on a flat sum or a long dispatch chain, and `guard` nests the rest of its block one level deeper each time. For a flat `a + b + c` the message ("nested more than 1000 levels deep") is also confusing.
2. The parser counter sits in `ParsePrimary`, but `ParseUnary` recurses into itself for `-`, `!`, `~` and `&` without going through it, so a long enough unary chain still runs the parser off the stack. The 18,390-`!` case in the description is caught only because the parser survives that depth and the checker then stops it.

A bound on the native stack itself would cover both without capping the shape of the tree. Record the stack address where parsing or checking starts, and report an error when the current frame is more than a fixed budget below it (comfortably under the thread's stack size). Check it in the same two places plus `ParseUnary`. That costs about as much code as this PR, works on every recursive path the check is placed on, and fires only on input that would otherwise crash. If you'd rather keep a count, it has to sit well above what generated code reaches (master's `check` handles 10,000 on all three shapes above), and it has to be in every self-recursive parse function.

Initial review by claude-opus-5-5:

Thanks for the careful lifecycle work, but I don't think this can merge in this form. The issue is the design, not the details, and the PR says itself that it needs maintainer agreement first. Concretely:

1. **It reverses a core rule of the language.** §11.2 opens with "Threads never share mutable memory". `docs/design/coroutines.md` §2.5 builds on that, and `docs/design/llm_frontier.md` §4.3 already plans how shared memory should enter: a `par for` that is race-free by proof, so no new runtime objects or locks are needed. This PR adds a second, runtime-checked model alongside it: 8 global builtins, 3 opaque types whose names become reserved (`struct SharedView { x: i64 }` in user code now fails with "reserved native type name"), and a new exception to the flat-argument rule for `thread_fn`. That's a direction for the language to decide in an issue or a `docs/design/` note before anyone writes code. Once it ships, it is hard to take back.

2. **It doesn't give the main benefit shared memory exists for.** Every `memory_read`/`memory_write` is a runtime call that takes one process-wide mutex (`gs_shared_mutex`), even when each borrow covers a disjoint range. Measured on Windows with clang-cl 22 at -O2, each worker writing 2M u64s into its own disjoint borrow:

   | workers | wall time |
   |---|---|
   | 1 | 26 ms |
   | 2 | 61 ms |
   | 4 | 200 ms |
   | 8 | 899 ms |

   So 8 workers do 8× the work in 35× the time. Copying chunks through queues, which the language already supports, would beat this.

3. **View records are never freed before `shared_close`, and every registry operation scans all of them.** A loop doing `shared_release(shared_borrow(shared_view(o, 0, 8)))` slows down quadratically: 272, 964, 1787 and 3011 ms for each successive batch of 20,000. Once `GS_SHARED_MAX` (1,048,576) records have been created, it aborts with "out of memory creating shared view".

4. **An overlapping borrow aborts instead of waiting.** Two workers that want the same range therefore crash or not depending on scheduling, and they need queues to coordinate anyway.

5. **Repository hygiene.** `docs/pr-drafts/` and `docs/readiness/` are notes about the PR process and don't belong in the tree. `docs/native_memory.md` isn't linked from anything and describes itself as a candidate awaiting agreement.

If the goal is fast shared-array parallelism, the first step is the `par for` design in llm_frontier.md §4.3. If there's a use case that `par for` and queues can't cover, an issue describing that use case would be the place to start.

Initial analysis by claude-opus-5-5:

These are all fair; that section compresses spec §3.3 and Appendix C too far. The actual answers:

- **varint**: a LEB128 integer, only explained later (tutorial §8). As a length it takes 1 byte up to 127 elements, 2 up to 16383, up to 10 for the full range. "Usually" means "for short arrays". The table should link forward.
- **`T[..k]` "inline"**: room for all `k` elements is reserved inside whatever holds it (a struct field, an array element), and the array uses 0 to `k` of them. "Small length" means the length field is the smallest unsigned type that fits `k` (`u8` up to 255, etc.). It is not a limit on `k`: `u8[..300]` works.
- **Length vs capacity**: `.len` is like `size()`. `.cap` (limited arrays only) is like `capacity()`, except it never changes: pushing past it aborts rather than reallocating. Resizables have no `.cap`; they're bounded by their data stack's reservation.
- **`[>..]` / `[>..<]`**: agreed, they should be marked in the table. Their elements top a data stack of their own and their length header is kept by the owner, so "`[metadata][elements]` in every one of them" doesn't really describe them.
- **Alignment**: everything is packed, no padding; loads and stores may be unaligned, which is cheap on x86-64 and ARM64 (spec §3.2, Appendix C.2). Structs have an explicit `pad` where you want alignment.
- **Freezing**: no inference. A growable array keeps its stack until its owner's scope ends. Nothing else needs to go "on top" of it, since other values use other stacks, which are just address-space reservations. To keep a finished array compact, copy it into a `T[]`: `let done: i64[] = copy(grow);`.

Suggested change: rework the table (forward link for varint, say what "small length" means, mark the two resizable rows with a footnote) and add three short points under it: len vs cap, packing/alignment, and copying a finished resizable into a `T[]`.

Initial analysis by claude-opus-5-5:

Thanks for the measurements and the comparison project. The core request, a verified view instead of a verified copy, fits naturally next to `bytes_of`/`from_bytes`. But there's a soundness issue in the proposed signature, and mmap needs more design than the issue suggests.

**`view_bytes` needs the bytes frozen, not just viewed read-only.** A `const u8[:]` doesn't stop writes through its owner: `var a: u8[>..] = ...; let s: const u8[:] = a[..]; a[0] = 9;` compiles and runs. If a view were verified over `a`, a later write to `a` could rewrite a verified link to an arbitrary offset, which is exactly what the verifier exists to prevent (`docs/design/serialization.md` §2). So the rule has to be about the *root*: the bytes must come from storage nothing can write while the view lives, e.g. a `let` binding of a `const` type (`let buf: const u8[>..] = ...;` rejects both writes and `push`) or static data. With that rule, `view_bytes<T[>..]>(bytes) -> const T[:], bool` is what you describe: same framing and verifier, no copy.

**Index types mostly already work.** `from_bytes` checks each `u32 in files` against the global array's current length, and those arrays never shrink, so a view can do the same. Indices into *another view* would be a separate feature; suggest leaving that out.

**mmap is the hard part:**
1. On Linux/macOS a mapping isn't a snapshot: another process writing or truncating the file changes or invalidates bytes already verified (SIGBUS on truncation). rkyv lives with this because memmap2's `Mmap::map` is `unsafe`; Goose has no such escape hatch. Windows can deny write sharing; POSIX only has advisory locks.
2. Goose has no destructors (`docs/design/ownership.md`). A mapping that unmaps itself at scope exit is one, and an explicit unmap while views exist is a use-after-free. This is the open resource-lifetime question in `owning_dynamic_data.md` option C.

The direction that fits the memory model is mapping into a data-stack region so the result is an ordinary array released like any other; on Windows that needs placeholder reservations, the same runtime change #191 ran into. So mmap stays on the list, deferred.

**Cheap wins now:**
- `read_file` (`gs_os_read_file` in `src/runtime/runtime_os.h`) reads in 64 KB chunks through a stack buffer and appends, copying twice and growing incrementally. Sizing the file first and reading straight into the destination is a small runtime fix and should take a chunk out of your 27 ms.
- Loading inside a helper so the read buffer dies after `from_bytes`, then `os::trim_memory()`, gets steady-state resident memory to ~1× today (peak during load stays 2×).

**Segmented verification:** suggest not; "loaded means verified" is worth keeping (serialization.md §4). An application can get the same effect by storing an image per segment and verifying each on first use.

Summary: `read_file` fix low cost / some benefit; `view_bytes` with a frozen-root rule medium cost / high benefit for this use case; mmap high cost, deferred.

`mmap` is an independent design problem. The big question is where this mmap memory would go. It can't easily be just a chunk of memory that lives outside Goose's stack memory, because I don't think we can have slices pointing to such memory, and/or managing its lifetime would be very different from all other slices. Making the result of `mmap` be an actual Goose stack would also be complicated, needing it to be a language feature almost (the compiler would need to know about it). We currently don't have dynamically allocated stacks (besides threads). Also it would possibly have a different size than other stacks.

My hunch is that the easiest path may be to research if the compiler could handle a special kind of `T[:]` type whose lifetime comes from a external memory creation function like mmap.

I don't think there's anything fundamental against allowing generics for a worker function, because in the end this compiles down to similar code as manually duplicated workers.

It is somewhat dangerous since a `thread_fn` is heavyweight: it compiles as a "separate program" for all functions it uses, so liberally using different generic arguments could mean increased compile times and code bloat.

Passing a generic function argument is only one way of specifying custom behavior for each worker, you could also use an `enum` for example that specifies the worker type. Maybe coroutines will soon provide another.

Most importantly though, the intent behind this change goes against what the concurrency model was designed for. This was meant to be a model where workers are all interchangeable, i.e. they can all do all of the work, and the contents of Q items they pick up make for different kinds of work to be done. This makes it flexible and optimal: one worker per core gets you maximum work done on any kind of hardware.

Making specialized workers that only do one kind of job, in contrast, may be a bad fit for a machine that has more or less cores than the amount of specialists.

Summary: you want to make the *work* polymorphic, not the *worker*.

I generally like the idea of allowing constant values as generic arguments, C++ and other languages have it obviously and it is useful there, so I think we should support it.

The field type may be something we eventually need for other reasons. It could be a 3rd template arg, but also worth considering if a feature similar to C++'s `decltype` is not more general, i.e. `decltype(dst.A)`.

Commit 1 (the server and the formatter on the compile thread) is a clear win and can go in as is. Commits 2 and 3 work, but most of their 23 `StackLow()` sites exist only because each one is the last thing between its pass and a crash, so every future pass that recurses with the program's nesting needs one too. Most of them can go if the overflow itself is caught.

**1. Bug: `ParseFnBody` frees nested functions that are still in the body.** It records `nfunctions` when the body starts, not per statement as `ParseBlockBody` does. On `TooDeep` it deletes every function declared in the body so far, including those declared by earlier statements, which stay in `b->stmts` before `brokenat` and still get checked and indexed. With

```
fn f() -> i64 {
    fn g() -> i64 { 41 }
    let y: bool = g();
    (((... 200,000 deep ... 1 )))
}
fn main() { print(f()); }
```

the server (Windows Release and Debug builds of 9c7aeacc) reports a spurious `unknown function: g`, and the outline lists `main` nested inside `f`: `g`'s `FnDecl` now points at the freed memory `main`'s `SFunction` took over.

**2. Catch the overflow once, on the compile thread.** The runtime already does this for generated programs (`gs_fault_filter` / `gs_fault_handler` in runtime_impl.h): a vectored handler plus `SetThreadStackGuarantee` on Windows, and on POSIX `sigaltstack` plus a `SIGSEGV`/`SIGBUS` handler that claims only faults inside the thread's own stack bounds and passes anything else to the previous handler. The same ~70 lines in `CompilerThread::Run` print `error: nested too deep for the compiler's stack` and exit 1. Every pass on that thread is then covered, including ones not written yet. `StackLow()` checks stop being needed to prevent crashes and become optional, for a source location or to keep going.

**3. Then one check pays for itself: `Descend`.** For the shapes generated code makes, the checker uses the most stack per level in a release build, so it runs out first, and a check there gives a located error. Keep `CheckSpecBodyOnce` as on master. The rest can go: the parser's `TooDeep`/`ParseFnBody`/`ParseTopDecl` changes, `Clone`, `ConstIntValue`/`ConstExprNames`, `SubstRaw`, `ValidateType`, both in resolve.h, both in the expansion binder, the three in codegen, `dumpcut` and the `Format` try/catch, `Ast::stackerror`, `StackErrors`, and `rootstack`/`stackat`. That last heuristic only chooses between two messages. It can be replaced by putting `Descend`'s floor 1 MB below the call path's (`StackPointer() + (1 << 20) < stackfloor`). A body that crosses the floor is then reported as the call path by `CheckSpecBodyOnce`, and only one that goes 1 MB past it is reported as nesting. Without that offset, `call_chain_too_deep` gets the nesting message.

The marsaglia method for rand_gaussian is painfully slow, I believe that a modern language (in the age of LLMs) should start with the best algorithms ootb.

Yours ofcourse is correct, but it throws away half the work: every accepted pair gives two independent normals, and `v * f` is discarded. Keeping it would mean storing a cached value inside `rng`, which complicates the generator state. I'd skip that and go straight to the Ziggurat method (Marsaglia & Tsang, J. Stat. Software, 2000), which needs no extra state and is much faster.

Right now each call costs about 2.5 uniforms on average, plus a `log`, a `sqrt` and a division. The Ziggurat splits the half-Gaussian into 128 or 256 strips of equal area, using tables computed once. About 99% of the time it needs one random integer, one multiply and one compare. Some of the integer's bits pick the strip, one bit gives the sign, and the rest is the value. Only the curved edge of a strip (one `exp` compare) and the tail past the last strip (an exponential rejection loop) need more work. Put those two cases in a separate function so the fast path stays small.

Read Doornik (2005), "An Improved Ziggurat Method", too: the original reuses the same bits for the index and the value, which creates a correlation, and the paper shows how to avoid it. Generate the tables with a separate script and check that the strip areas are equal. Before timing anything, check the moments, run a KS test, and especially check the tails, for example the fraction of |x| > 4 over 10⁸ samples, since that's where Ziggurat bugs show up. Then compare speed against this version using the same `rand_flt`. 

for a good reference implementation Julia's `randn` (`Random/src/normal.jl`) is a clean 256-strip implementation worth considering.

I agree with @aardappel, @binji, and @francescoalemanno: the compiler shouldn't parse C headers, and writing explicit `.goose` declarations (by hand, with an LLM, or with a generator tool) fits Goose.

The problem I hit in `goose-wing` that led to PR #235 is what happens *after* you write explicit `.goose` declarations for a header like `<emmintrin.h>`, `<wmmintrin.h>`, or `<arm_neon.h>`:

1. Header macros and `static inline` functions have no library symbol. `extern "lib" { ... }` binds via `dlopen` and `dlsym`, while a bare `extern fn` emits a freestanding C prototype (`extern a16_u8 _mm_xor_si128(a16_u8, a16_u8);`) without an `#include`. That fails on C macros and clashes with `static inline` definitions in the header.
2. Vector and intrinsic types conflict with `#pragma pack(push, 1)`. As noted in #121, Goose keeps its own types 1-byte aligned (`a16_u8`) so structs and frames avoid over-aligned stack ABI bugs. `<emmintrin.h>` declares `__m128i`. Without a conversion at the call site (`type m128i = u8[16] = "__m128i";` emitting a `memcpy` helper at the C call while keeping `m128i` a plain `u8[16]` in Goose), you still have to write a `.c` shim for every intrinsic.
3. Immediate operands and target attributes. Intrinsics like `_mm_clmulepi64_si128(a, b, imm8)` require `imm8` to be a literal constant in C (`const` parameter), and GCC and Clang reject inlining them unless the calling C function has `__attribute__((target("...")))`.

PR #235 keeps declarations explicit in `.goose`, just like `extern "SDL2" { ... }`. It teaches `extern "<header.h>"` to emit the `#include`, map `u8[16]` to and from `__m128i` (and slices or refs to pointers) at the call site, and handle `const` immediate arguments and `target_has` dispatch so `.goose` packages can call SIMD or header-only C APIs without `.c` wrapper files.

(PR #235 also adds fixed-length slice windows `s[lo..+N]` -> `T[N]` as a separate first commit, for reading and writing fixed-size blocks like `u8[16]` from a slice in pure Goose code.)

Review by claude-fable-5-1:

Looks good to merge. The runtime side is correct as far as I can see, and the cost to programs that never call `trim` is zero. Two points on semantics, one of which wants a sentence in the docs.

**Stale views now change without an allocation.** The documented pool contract (spec §9.4, and stdlib.md's "freed references/views remain valid and can observe replacement values") is that a stale view reads a *valid value of the correct type*, which zeros satisfy. But the de-facto behaviour today is stronger: `free_slice` writes no element bytes and the tree lives in `nodes`, so the only thing that ever writes a freed run is the pool handing it out again. After `trim`, bytes change with no allocation in between; the new test relies on exactly that (`b[b.len - 1] == 0` through a stale view). The `trim` paragraph in stdlib.md says "they read back as zeros" but frames it as harmless. Suggest adding a sentence along the lines of: *reading a freed run is an application error, but without `trim` such a read sees the run's old bytes until the pool reuses it; after `trim` it sees zeros, so adding a `trim` call can change the behaviour of a program that is not clean of such reads.*

**Relative references.** Safe for `u8`: no reference of any kind can live in `u8` items, nothing typed sits over a `u8` pool's bytes (`from_bytes` copies; `bytes_of` goes the other way and is read-only), a pool-relative `u8&<u32 in p.items>` held elsewhere still targets a valid `u8`, and only pages strictly inside a free span are discarded. For the extension to other zero-valid element types that `owning_dynamic_data.md` sketches, "no non-optional reference" needs to say explicitly that it includes self-relative ones. An optional relref reads offset 0 as null, which is fine, but a non-optional self-relative reference has no null sentinel: spec §3.9 says offset 0 denotes the address of its own field, so a zeroed one is a `T&` pointing at its own offset field, which is type confusion. Worth a few words in the note now so the rule is right before anyone extends it.

Code notes:

- The walk's visit count aborts at `nodes.len` visits and valid node numbers are `1..len-1`, so one repeat trips it; `l` never exceeds the checked height, so the path arrays cannot overflow.
- On Windows the fault handler commits on any touch inside the usable part and only ever raises `committed`, so stale reads below the mark recommit and a later `trim_memory` stays correct; `MEM_DECOMMIT` on already-decommitted pages is a no-op.
- The `gs_trim_memory` refactor is behaviour-preserving on all three platforms.
- Nit: one line of the new stdlib.md paragraph ("Like `trim_memory`, it is explicit: ...") runs well past the wrap width of the surrounding text.
- The `trim` name resolves by argument type, so it is fine as is.
We may eventually want to reorganize these docs, but for now this is a good fix!

Initial analysis by claude-opus-5-5:

**Not a bug.** In `(-2147483647 - 1)`, `2147483647` is an `int`, so `-2147483647` is an `int`. Subtracting 1 gives -2147483648, which is `INT_MIN` and representable in a 32-bit `int`. **Partly right, mostly harmless.**

Initial analysis by claude-opus-5-5:

**Reproduced on master (e0b12259)** in three forms:
- the holder version, as posted;
- the plain-reference variant (`node: Node&`, with the back edge passing `out[i]`);
- that variant with `out` passed in as a `Node&[>..<]&` pool parameter. This one fails with "passes node rooted differently from the cycle's entry call".

**Reading of the spec:** this is the "Further refinements are future work" edge of §7.8, not a checker bug. Neither threaded-parameter paragraph covers these shapes:
- The first needs every back edge to pass the parameter on, and `eval(p.b, out[i])` doesn't.
- The second needs the argument on *every* call to be read through a threaded parameter or a pool. The entry call passes `root`, which is rooted exactly at a local of `main` but is not read through a pool.

**A sound refinement would accept both shapes.** Anything read out of storage owned outside the cycle is itself rooted outside the cycle. That storage is a global, a pool parameter, or a local of an enclosing non-cycle function, and the cycle store rule is precisely what keeps cycle-local roots out of it. So consider a parameter whose argument at every call is one of these:
- (a) at the entry call, a reference rooted outside the cycle;
- (b) the parameter passed on;
- (c) a reference read out of storage owned outside the cycle.

Such a parameter points outside the cycle in every activation, so what it holds may be stored into storage owned outside the cycle.

**Suggestion:**
- **Plain reference parameter:** worth doing. It is the natural tree-walk shape over `std::json`'s `Node`. The rule is a small generalization of the existing second paragraph: treat "read out of outside-owned storage" like "read through a pool", and an entry argument rooted at an outside local like one read through a pool. The spec text barely changes.
- **By-value holder parameter (`v: Val` with a reference inside):** the same argument applies. However, it needs the threaded-class tracking to follow references inside by-value payloads, which means more machinery in the hardest part of the checker to audit. I'd do it only if the reference-parameter case generalizes cheaply. Until then, the index workaround, or a `Node&` parameter with a separate tag, covers it.

**Cost and benefit:** moderate cost, because this is a soundness-critical area and needs adversarial tests. For example, a back edge passing a reference to a cycle local packed inside a holder must stay rejected. Moderate benefit, because reference-linked trees are the stdlib's own shape.

The repro would make a good fixture under `test/`, once the intended behaviour is decided.
